paragraphs: Once there was a poor woodcutter who worked from early morning until late at night. When he had finally saved some money, he said to his son, “You are my only child. I will spend the money I have earned by the sweat of my brow on your education. If you learn an honest trade, you can support me in my old age, when my limbs grow stiff and I must stay at home.” The boy went to a high school and studied so diligently that his teachers praised him. He stayed there a long time. But after he had completed two classes, before he had mastered everything, the little money his father had earned was gone, and he had to return home. “Ah,” his father said sadly, “I cannot give you any more. In these hard times, I cannot earn a farthing beyond what we need for our daily bread.” “Dear Father,” his son replied, “don’t worry about it. If it is God’s will, it will turn out well for me. I will soon get used to it.” When his father prepared to go into the forest to earn money helping to pile, stack and chop wood, the son said, “I will come and help you.” “No, my son,” his father said. “It would be hard for you. You are not used to heavy work and could not bear it. Besides, I have only one axe and no money to buy another.” “Go to the neighbour,” his son said. “He will lend you his axe until I have earned one of my own.” His father borrowed the neighbour’s axe, and at daybreak the next morning they went into the forest together. The son helped his father cheerfully and energetically. When the sun was directly overhead, his father said, “We will rest and eat our midday meal. Then we shall work well again.” The son picked up his bread. “You rest, Father,” he said. “I’m not tired. I’ll walk around the forest a little and look for birds’ nests.” “Oh, you fool,” his father said. “Why do you want to run about? You’ll be tired afterwards and unable to lift your arm. Stay here and sit beside me.” But the son went into the forest, eating his bread, cheerful and happy. He peered into the green branches to see whether he could find a bird’s nest. He wandered back and forth looking for one until he reached an enormous, dangerous-looking oak. It was certainly hundreds of years old, and even five men could not have reached around it. He stopped and looked. “Many birds must have nested in that,” he thought. Suddenly he seemed to hear a voice. He listened and made out someone crying in a very muffled voice, “Let me out! Let me out!” He looked around but saw nothing. Still, he thought the voice came from the ground. “Where are you?” he called. “Down here among the oak’s roots,” the voice answered. “Let me out! Let me out!” The student loosened the earth beneath the tree and searched among the roots until he found a glass bottle in a little hollow. He lifted it to the light and saw a frog-shaped creature jumping up and down inside. “Let me out! Let me out!” it cried again. Suspecting no harm, the student pulled out the cork. At once a spirit rose from the bottle and began to grow. It grew so quickly that in a few moments a terrible figure stood before him, half as tall as the tree beside him. “Do you know,” it cried in a dreadful voice, “what your reward is for letting me out?” “No,” the student answered fearlessly. “How should I know?” “Then I will tell you,” the spirit cried. “I must strangle you for it.” “You should have told me that sooner,” the student said. “Then I would have left you shut up. But my head will stay where it is, whatever you may do. More than one person must have a say about that.” “More than one here, more than one there,” the spirit said. “You shall get the reward you have earned. Do you think I was shut in there for so long as a favour? No, it was my punishment. I am the mighty Mercurius. Whoever frees me, I must strangle.” “Gently,” the student replied. “Not so fast. First I must know that you really were shut inside that little bottle and that you are the right spirit. If you can get back in, I will believe you, and then you can do whatever you like with me.” “That is a trivial feat,” the spirit said proudly. He drew himself together, becoming as small and thin as before, and crept through the same opening, right down the bottle’s neck. The instant he was inside, the student pushed the cork back in and threw the bottle among the oak’s roots, into its old place. The spirit had been tricked.

The student was about to return to his father when the spirit cried pitifully, “Oh, let me out! Oh, let me out!” “No,” the student answered. “Not a second time! Someone who has already tried to kill me will not be set free by me, now that I have caught him again.” “If you free me,” the spirit said, “I will give you enough to keep you in plenty for the rest of your life.” “No,” the boy said. “You would deceive me as you did before.” “You are throwing away your own good fortune,” the spirit said. “I will not hurt you. I will reward you richly.” The student thought, “I’ll risk it. Perhaps he will keep his word. In any case, he will not get the better of me.” He pulled out the cork. The spirit rose from the bottle as before, stretched himself out, and grew as large as a giant. “Now you shall have your reward,” he said. He handed the student a little bag that looked like a sticking plaster. “Lay one end over a wound,” he said, “and the wound will heal. Rub steel or iron with the other end, and it will turn to silver.” “I must try that,” the student said. He went to a tree, tore off some bark with his axe, and rubbed the place with one end of the plaster. At once the bark closed up and healed. “Now everything is right,” he told the spirit, “and we can part.” The spirit thanked him for setting him free. The boy thanked the spirit for his gift and returned to his father.

“Where have you been running about?” his father asked. “Why have you forgotten your work? I said from the start you would never manage anything.” “Don’t worry, Father. I’ll make it up.” “Make it up indeed!” his father said angrily. “There’s no skill in that.” “Watch, Father. I’ll soon chop that tree until it splits.” He took his plaster, rubbed the axe with it, and struck a mighty blow. But the iron had turned to silver, and the edge bent. “Oh, Father, look what a bad axe you’ve given me! It’s bent right over.” His father was horrified. “Ah, what have you done? Now I must pay for it, and I have no money. That is all the good your work has done me.” “Don’t be angry,” his son said. “I will soon pay for the axe.” “Oh, you blockhead!” his father cried. “What will you pay with? You have nothing except what I give you. Your head is full of students’ tricks, but you know nothing about woodcutting.” After a while the student said, “Father, I really cannot work any more. We had better take the day off.” “What?” his father answered. “Do you think I will sit with my hands in my lap like you? I must keep working, but you can go home.” “Father, this is my first time in this forest. I don’t know the way on my own. Please come with me.” His father’s anger had cooled, and at last he let himself be persuaded and went home with him. Then he said, “Go and sell your damaged axe and see what you can get for it. I must earn the difference to pay the neighbour.” His son took the axe to a goldsmith in town. The goldsmith tested it, put it on the scales, and said, “It is worth four hundred thalers. I don’t have that much here.” “Give me what you have,” the son said. “I will lend you the rest.” The goldsmith gave him three hundred thalers and owed him another hundred. The son went home and said, “Father, I have the money. Go and ask the neighbour what he wants for his axe.” “I already know,” the old man answered. “One thaler and six groschen.” “Then give him two thalers and twelve groschen. That is double, and enough. Look, I have plenty of money.” He gave his father a hundred thalers. “You shall never be in need,” he said. “Live as comfortably as you like.” “Good heavens!” his father said. “Where did you get all these riches?” The student told him everything that had happened, and how trusting his luck had brought him such success. With the money left over, he returned to the high school and continued his studies. Since he could heal every wound with his plaster, he became the most famous doctor in the whole world.
